#10422. The AI boom was built around Jensen Huang. What happens now?

Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

Jensen Huang is out, and the repercussions are just beginning

Who would have expected the AI Bubble to pop like this? Over an infidelity scandal. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia CEO Thursday, built the company that supplied the chips that made the AI boom possible. He had the foresight to see the AI revolution coming, and formed the strategy to lock AI researchers and enterprises into his company’s CUDA software stack. 

Huang also used Nvidia’s growing chip sales windfall to prop up the growing AI industry in a dangerous way, bankrolling a webwork of AI startups, suppliers, infrastructure players, and other chip customers. Now, with a crisis of confidence in the chip company at the center, the whole AI buildout could come under considerable strain and potentially unravel. 

With all this at stake, one might wonder why Nvidia’s board and other stakeholders would want Huang to resign. But Jensen Huang’s affairs were more than marital transgressions. At least one of them had national security and geopolitical dimensions–Huang’s relationship with a Singapore-based tech executive who goes by the name Alice Huang. Not only was she a suspected Chinese spy but her company, Megaspeed, was suspected by the Commerce Department of helping funnel restricted Nvidia chips to China, the U.S.’s main rival in the AI race.  

A New York Times investigation last year found that Megaspeed’s offices in Singapore and Malaysia were largely empty, and Commerce Department officials who spoke to The Times said they found boxes of restricted Nvidia chips in a Megaspeed facility in Malaysia. It’s long been the policy of the U.S. government to reserve the fastest AI chips, most of them made by Nvidia, for U.S. and U.S.-friendly AI labs. 

Alice Huang had  Chinese “honeypot” written all over her, but Jensen Huang never caught on, or chose not to. 

The second extramarital relationship to come to light is less harmful to Nvidia but establishes a pattern of infidelity that may go further than we currently know. It involved Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia VP who led Nvidia’s health industry business. That relationship, which had for months been discussed within Nvidia, was reported this week by the New York Times after reporters spoke to Nvidia employees. Nvidia’s code of conduct warns against employees “personal relationships” that might “create conflict.” 

It all seems so sudden. After months of hand wringing about the reality of the AI boom and the stability of the enormous amounts of investment money now being plowed into building out the infrastructure needed for AI, suddenly the man at the center of it all is gone, his 33 years of leading Nvidia over. And as Creative Strategies CEO Tim Bajarin told me, there’s nobody in the world with better field vision in the AI industry than Jensen Huang.

“For much of the last decade he was the industry’s main spokesperson, explaining to customers, partners, governments and investors where computing was going and why,” says Bajarin, a long-time Silicon Valley analyst who knows Huang. “Few executives in technology have played that role . . . that is a real loss, for NVIDIA and for the ecosystem around it.”

“Still, no one is irreplaceable, and the loss of a visionary is not the same as a change in strategy,” Bajarin says. “The vision Jensen laid out is already built into NVIDIA’s roadmap, its supply chain and its people, so we do not think his departure changes where the company is going.”

Possible successors to Huang may have some pieces of the picture, but none have vision into the human relationships and deep structural dependencies that have pushed it all forward. “His right-hand man and the one who executed Jensen’s strategy is Ian Buck,” Bajarin offers. Bajarin believes Buck could be a strong candidate to succeed Huang permanently. 

Still, Huang’s affairs and subsequent resignation have already destroyed some confidence in the enormous investment being made in the AI build out. Nvidia’s stock is already off 13%. But the industry, public, and governmental reaction to Huang’s departure may be just beginning, like the first ripples of a very large stone dropped into a pond.

The real reasons Anthropic is IPO’ing first, and OpenAI later

Anthropic and OpenAI will be the first two pure-play AI companies to tap the public markets through an initial public offering. Anthropic will likely list its stock (ticker symbol: “ANT”) first, potentially on November 19, while analysts expect OpenAI, which filed its own IPO paperwork confidentially in June, to wait until early next year.

The timing of these IPOs matters a lot because both companies operate in an extremely expensive business, and they’re competing for capital from the same pool of retail and institutional investors. Both are trying to raise money at valuations well above a trillion dollars amid growing concerns about rising interest rates, volatility in technology stocks, heightened scrutiny of AI company valuations, and a decidedly negative political environment.

All about compute

Still, no artificial intelligence bubble has popped—yet—so Anthropic and OpenAI may want to go public while conditions are (relatively) good. Harrison Rolfes, an analyst at PitchBook, says it may also be a question of necessity. Both companies remain focused on buying, leasing, or building as much computing capacity as they can, even decades into the future. For a long time, they’ve relied on venture capital money and debt to cover those costs, but as private capital becomes harder to come by, they need to tap the public markets.

That may be a more urgent issue for Anthropic than for OpenAI. “The compute bills come due in December,” Rolfes tells Fast Company. Anthropic has shown impressive revenue growth during 2026, putting some real numbers behind the $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion valuation the company has proposed. “By being at this current valuation at this current time they can retain the interest and then run the momentum into the IPO,” Rolfes says.

OpenAI likely bought itself some time with the sizable capital it raised in the private markets this year, Rolfes believes. In March, the company raised $122 billion, and a recent Reuters report says OpenAI is trying to raise additional capital at a valuation of more than $1.4 trillion, locking down commitments before the Anthropic IPO. OpenAI also has a broader range of revenue sources than Anthropic, including consumer subscriptions, a growing advertising business, and licensing agreements with partners like Microsoft. OpenAI’s revenue reportedly grew more than 50% to over $10 billion in the third quarter.

A straight story

OpenAI will have to tell a clear and compelling story when it goes public—one that can withstand the scrutiny of the public markets. In fact, earlier this year, OpenAI’s CFO, Sara Friar, reportedly cited the lack of such a story as one reason her company wouldn’t be ready for a 2026 IPO.

“OpenAI’s timeline is different, and that makes sense given the company it’s building,” Jyoti Bansal, AI investor and founder of the software delivery platform Harness, tells Fast Company. “It has a different structure and a much broader business to run, spanning consumer, enterprise, infrastructure, and hardware.” OpenAI will have to clarify whether it’s primarily a consumer AI or an enterprise AI company, or how focusing equally on both could enhance and not limit overall growth in the future.

Anthropic, on the other hand, may have a slightly easier story to tell. “The business leans toward enterprise, and enterprise revenue is the kind public investors tend to value: recurring, tied to usage, and connected to real workflows,” Bansal says. “When customers are running your models in production, for coding, support and internal agents, you have a story that holds up under public-market scrutiny.”

First-mover advantage

Anthropic could see real benefits from going public first. It could set the terms by which public investors evaluate frontier AI company stocks, establishing a pricing benchmark and common metrics for measuring short- and long-term success.

This could put OpenAI in an uncomfortable position. “The $1.25 trillion that they are asking for will be compared to whatever Anthropic trades at,” Rolfes says. “So that’s the issue that OpenAI is going to face because now you have a comparable and if they can’t match that then it’s only going to cause them to get a larger discount on their value.” If OpenAI wants to command a higher valuation than Anthropic and raise more money, it will have to clearly explain to investors why it should be valued or measured differently.

OpenAI, remember, was seen as “the leading AI company” for years after the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022. Much of that first-mover mojo is gone, but not all—it matters that millions of consumers had their first experience with AI through ChatGPT. Still, OpenAI could lose a little more mojo if it has to follow Anthropic to market.

“It puts them at a disadvantage in terms of listing first and capturing the mind share of people,” Rolfes says. “They used to be the go-to, but now if the name switches from OpenAI over to Anthropic, then it’s like, OK, maybe [Anthropic] will start to creep into the consumer mind share.”

The timing of an IPO doesn’t decide a company’s fate. In the long run, investors care more about quarter-to-quarter profitability and predictability. But pure-play AI companies are something new, and the timing of their IPOs may matter more. They have to spend unheard-of amounts of capital, some of it raised from the public markets, on infrastructure to stay competitive in the breakneck race to build state-of-the-art models. Any hiccup in plans to raise enough money for compute could leave an AI company behind in a race where catching up is exceedingly difficult. Meanwhile, its revenue opportunities—and potential shareholder returns—could shrink.

Anthropic’s new model built an operating system from an empty folder

In other Anthropic news, on Monday the AI giant released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model with different safeguards. In prerelease testing, the company says, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder; it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents for eight days and produced one that boots on a laptop, with drivers, file storage, windows, a login screen, and an installer. Given a one-paragraph prompt, it also designed three working electronic devices—a voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet—with circuit boards ready to manufacture in under a day. 

Netflix is calling its recommendations AI

Netflix began rolling out AI Discover, its first consumer feature branded as AI-powered, to a limited number of U.S. subscribers on supported smart TVs, Variety reported. Subscribers can choose from preset themes such as “Something Light,” “Scare Me,” and “Family Movie Night.” A “Tune Your Recommendations” button lets viewers keep a suggestion or block it from appearing again. The content is not available on kids’ profiles. Netflix has used machine learning to recommend content for years; now it’s using it to generate content.

OpenAI’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion

OpenAI’s quarterly revenue topped $10 billion for the first time, Bloomberg reported, a jump of roughly 50% from $6.7 billion in the second quarter, and the company’s adjusted operating margin narrowed from negative 150% to negative 109%. OpenAI’s annual revenue run rate now stands at $50 billion. Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $17 billion and said this week its run rate had reached $81 billion as of the end of October. (Note: the two companies calculate revenues differently: Anthropic counts the total spend on Claude models through cloud partner distributors, while OpenAI reports only its piece of the revenue-share).

The current feature is a beta and only available for Steam Deck, but it's coming to all users eventually.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Valve is adding framerate telemetry data to games so you can see what your hardware will manage in a given game before you buy it. The new initiative will start with the Steam Deck, but Valve has promised to bring the feature to more hardware in the future, presumably not only its Steam Machine but desktop gaming PCs more generally. The new feature shows players' average FPS on Steam Deck while playing the title, so customers can decide whether to invest without risking a purchase.

Valve already added the option to insert your hardware specifications when you write a review for a game, but an extremely small fraction of players actually write reviews, and from looking at reviews on recent Steam games, it seems like an even smaller fraction actually select to include their hardware specifications, for whatever reason.

The clever among you may have realized "but wait, PC games have settings you can adjust, so even the same hardware might deliver really different performance levels." Correct! And it's also exactly why Valve is doing this. Its Steam Deck Verified program requires a certain level of performance, and games can get marked as "Unsupported" if they don't reach that level, but some people may find them playable regardless. In other words, there's no one perfect standard for "playable performance," and thus Valve wants to let users decide for themselves.

Valve says that, at least for this early trial with Steam Deck data, that data is being filtered to only show data from Decks that are set to the default frame limit. The firm doesn't make any attempt to account for custom in-game settings, yet it says that "despite this, [Valve has] found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges," after accounting for the unusual effects of vertical sync.

So what if you don't have a Steam Deck? Well, Valve says it sees this update (adding the Steam Deck framerate data) as "a stepping stone toward providing framerate data for more devices than just Steam Deck." Obviously, that includes Valve's own Steam Machine mini-desktop and Steam Frame VR headset, but presumably it will extend to folks on standard gaming PCs (whether desktop or laptop)

It's not clear whether desktop performance data will be matched by graphics card, some combination of GPU and CPU, or multiple factors, but either way, there's no question that this is yet another feature that sets Steam as a storefront above its competitors. If you'd like to opt in, you'll have to join the Steam Client Beta for now; Valve says the feature is coming to all users "in the future," though.

#10419. Burnout is a workplace safety hazard. It’s time to start treating it like one

Burnout is a huge workplace issue: the low engagement that comes with it costs every business affected a fortune. Worse yet, its effects on workers are deleterious to the point where it can literally lead to death.

Yet in my experience, most leaders consider “burnout” an HR line item to be managed by a wellness program. It’s hard to know how to jolt people out of this mindset, but if I were a CEO (and I am), I’d be very concerned about potential industrial manslaughter charges coming my way at worst, and shareholders rightfully wondering why I am failing to manage the main thing that’s materially impairing productivity at best.

Burnout is a workplace safety hazard—and needs to be governed as one. 

The World Health Organization defines burnout as the result of “chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.” It’s a costly hazard that claims at least twice as many lives as workplace accidents. Long working hours alone led to an estimated 750,000 deaths from stroke and heart disease in 2016, more than twice the 360,000 people killed by workplace injuries, according to a report from WHO and the International Labour Organization. In the USA, workplace stressors are estimated to kill 120,000 people a year. 

Outside of the devastating human impact, the toll burnout takes on commercial performance should be triggering emergency board meetings all over the world. At an estimated cost of US $5 million a year for a company of 1,000 employees, it would be reasonable to ask very direct questions of the executive about their plans to arrest the poorly designed workplace practices that lead to burnout. 

Maybe the questions could start with who decided that it was okay to spend more than half of your working week in meetings or managing the almost 600 emails and more than 750 Teams messages knowledge workers field every week. Perhaps some questions about what the executive has done to deliberately design the working week toward outcomes—not admin. 

Burnout and chronic workplace stress come from the health of a company’s culture, and culture is almost universally dismissed, neglected or delegated to HR: A function with no formal training in organizational culture, no resources to shape it, and by its very station, no authority over the leadership behavior that does.

So, when an organization is faced with a growing number of employees taking chronic work stress-related leave—in Australia, the median time off for a serious mental health claim is almost five times that of other serious workplace injuries—it looks for a button to press, inside a function it believes has the answer. But doesn’t. 

HR has never had the answer and never will. The organizations that shape their culture with intention, and deliberately look at the accidental practices we’ve inherited from antique cultures, don’t start with HR. They look directly at:

  • the board, which needs to be asking the right questions, in line with increasing regulation and on behalf of shareholders looking for optimal productivity
  • the CEO, who is entirely accountable for the productivity and performance of the organization
  • the leaders who shape culture through the expectations they set, the practices they perpetuate, the consequences they apply for culture drift, and the chronic workplace issues they walk past every single day

CEOs and organizations never set out to burn their people out. It’s more a matter of ‘out of sight, out of mind’ and neglect. Neglecting the implications of workplace practices, neglecting better ways of working that are confirmed by research rather than the assumptions of a post-industrial era, and neglecting to look through the human lens at a growing contributor to cardiovascular incidents and death by suicide.

Whether leaders look at burnout through a productivity lens or from a human suffering perspective, the situation is clear. Leaders are enabling the ongoing, systemic impairment of commercial performance at the cost of human lives…and feeling OK about it because they’ve passed a memo to HR to invest in a wellness program or resilience training.

Thankfully, regulators and standard setters understand the crisis better and have begun something of a reckoning. ISO 45003 became the first international standard for managing psychological health and safety at work in 2021, and the US Surgeon General’s Framework for Workplace Mental Health and Well-Being names protection from harm, psychological safety included, as its first essential.

Australia has moved from guidance to enforcement. Every Australian state and territory now requires employers to identify and manage psychosocial hazards in the same way as physical ones, and in December 2025, Australia’s Department of Defence became the first federal employer convicted for failing to manage psychosocial risk.

Burnout is, quite literally, an existential risk. It’s time organizations truly started acting like it.

If this article raises concerns for you or someone you know, support is available. In the USA, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline on 988. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14.

#10418. Wyze’s new door lock has speedy fingerprint recognition and 12-month battery life

Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. Rather, this is a smart lock designed for your standard single-bore latch, meaning it’s available for doors that other smart locks aren’t compatible with. You can still have a deadbolt, but you’ll need enough space for both (per Wyze’s guidelines below).

The Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze says recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second. It uses local storage for biometric data and works to improve that data with each successful unlock.

The PIN has a clever feature (though it’s presented in somewhat poor taste) that lets you input random digits before or after your actual code to prevent onlookers from being able to see your code. There’s also a physical key backup as well as a USB-C input on the outside in the case that the battery dies – Wyze says it lasts about 12 months on a charge using eight AA batteries.

The Wyze Lever Lock is available today for $99.98 and shipping immediately.

#10415. Can we please stop calling it a ‘honey trap’?

When Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on November 8 that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, there’s a phrase that quickly became omnipresent in the media: Huang had been the victim of a “honey trap,” laid by Alice Huang (no relation), a Singapore-based tech executive identified as a Chinese spy by U.S. intelligence agencies.

“Honey trap,” seriously?

The story behind the phrase is that a good, hardworking man was minding his own business when a serpent of a woman lured him off the righteous path by dishonest means and propositions he, being a man, simply couldn’t refuse. It is assumed that male sex drive is some kind of force of nature that no adult can reasonably be expected to control. So there’s a double sexist stereotype here. Can a 63-year-old billionaire CEO really be supposed to have no say over his sex life? Like a bear wouldn’t be able to resist honey?

Anyone who, like me, grew up in the 1980s knows a close relative of this idea: the “homewrecker,” a word aimed at the other woman and never at the husband who cheated. One of the decade’s most successful films, Fatal Attraction (1987), tells the story of a married man (Michael Douglas) whose affair turns into a nightmare when the woman (Glenn Close) refuses to stay discreet and starts asking for more. The film portrays the mistress as mentally unstable and dangerous. The film ends with the wife killing the mistress and family values restored. The husband’s betrayal is never really an issue. I’m ashamed to admit that when I first watched it, some time in the 1990s, I sided completely with the poor husband, hounded by a woman the film had led me to see as a witch.

Both ideas have their roots in Genesis, where Adam, asked why he ate the forbidden fruit, answers that the woman gave it to him. It is easy scapegoating: powerful men keep their reputation for rationality while some snake of a woman takes the blame for their lapses of judgment. There’s a paradox that I find difficult to swallow. For centuries, women were judged too foolish to vote or hold office, yet the same culture credits them with enough cunning to bring down kings and CEOs. Men, meanwhile, are supposed to be fit to lead nations and markets while being too weak to resist the first temptation that comes their way.

Deadly clichés

The term comes from spy fiction: dictionaries credit John le Carré with popularizing “honey trap” in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy in 1974. Espionage has long been a man’s world, and in its novels a female spy is very often a seductress. Real Cold War espionage looked quite different, since East Germany’s best-known seduction program used men, so-called “Romeo” agents sent west to seduce secretaries with access to government files. 

In the Nvidia story, much of the coverage of Alice Huang also draws on images Western culture has attached to Asian women for more than a century: the mysterious seductress, the Dragon Lady. In the U.S., they go back at least to the Page Act of 1875, the country’s first restrictive federal immigration law, which was enforced on the presumption that Chinese women were prostitutes. Any woman arriving from Asia had to prove she wasn’t one.

In March 2021, a white man killed eight people at three Atlanta-area spas, six of them Asian women, and police relayed his description of his victims as “sources of temptation.” Asian women end up being blamed for men’s desire. And Atlanta showed that this cliché can be deadly. Coverage casting Alice Huang as a seductress is anything but harmless.

Nobody trapped the CEO

A CEO’s sexual relationship with someone working for one of his company’s biggest customers is a clear conflict of interest. Alice Huang’s employer, Megaspeed, is said to have bought about $4.8 billion of Nvidia hardware over the past two years. In most companies, a sales manager sleeping with a key client’s buyer would be expected to disclose it and hand the account to a colleague. Nobody would describe that sales manager as “trapped,” and the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies, who has far more power, deserves no more indulgence.

The phrase also shrinks Alice Huang: if she is only “honey,” she cannot be much of a professional. Yet she ran a business that bought chips at enormous scale, and if the allegations hold, she will have to answer for export violations and espionage, serious crimes committed with the very agency the word denies her.

Call it what it is

The honey trap trope has consequences in the workplace. In 2019, a LeanIn.Org and SurveyMonkey survey found that 60% of male managers in the U.S. were uncomfortable mentoring, working one-on-one with, or socializing with a woman, and 36% of men said they had avoided doing so for fear of how it would look. A woman alone with a powerful man is seen as a danger to him, even though she is far more likely to be the one harassed. She also pays in lost dinners, business trips and sponsorship, the informal moments that decide who gets promoted.

Other words would be more honest. A CEO had an affair with an executive at one of his largest customers, a woman U.S. officials reportedly believe was working for Chinese intelligence, and his board is now examining whether the relationship compromised the company. It is less catchy than “honey trap,” but it treats both people as adults responsible for their choices. Isn’t that the standard any employee would expect?

#10414. Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

LangSmith is closed-source and restricts self-hosting to enterprise licenses, teams that run their own LLMOps stack and want to keep traces on their own servers need an alternative. To find the best fit, we set a baseline by tracing a small TypeScript agent (equipped with two tools) in LangSmith Cloud. Then, we ran the exact same agent through Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Opik, and AcruxCore using each platform's recommended TypeScript setup. All tests were run on November 5, 2026, and we pulled every trace back through each tool's API to verify the data.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree for the test prompt: a single agent span containing three LLM calls and two tool calls. The real differences between them come down to how much boilerplate code you have to write, how spans are typed, whether costs are tracked, and the overall server footprint.

Why Teams Look for a LangSmith Alternative

LangSmith remains the best choice if you already use LangChain and allow cloud hosting—it required just 25 lines of code in our test. The alternatives below are for teams that don't fit that profile.

To test these platforms, we built a simple customer support agent equipped with two tools:

Both tools use static fixture data to ensure every test run is identical. The agent runs a standard loop: it prompts the model, executes any requested tools, and stops once the model provides a final answer.

We tested the agent with three specific prompts to see how the tracing handled different levels of complexity:

For our comparison, we focused entirely on the third question because it generates a robust, multi-step trace.

Under the hood, the agent uses the standard openai package to call the qwen3.8-flash model. We originally picked this model based on its reliable tool-calling behavior during early probing thought it once skipped a tool call later.

We used LangSmith as our baseline. By tracing the agent there first, we created a checklist of every field it captured, and we judged all the alternatives against that exact list.

For setup, we followed the recommended TypeScript approach from each tool's documentation. Phoenix didn't have specific instructions for using its register() helper with OpenAI in TypeScript, so we adapted the pattern from their Anthropic guide.

Here is the agent with no tracing. Each tool section adds one tracing file that imports these files and changes nothing in them.

LangSmith traces the plain openai package with two helpers. wrapOpenAI records each model call, and traceable records your own functions. Without traceable on the run and the tools, wrapOpenAI alone gave three separate root runs and no tool runs.

This file adds 25 lines and removes 3, and installs one package.

LangSmith showed one root run with five children in call order: LLM, get_order_status, LLM, get_refund_policy, LLM. Every field it recorded became a row of the checklist table under "Results". Cost appeared only after a custom price entry. In our error run the failing tool was marked as an error, but the root stayed success: traceable turned the throw into a rejected promise that our agent did not await, so the agent carried on and answered.

Langfuse self-hosts as six containers, including ClickHouse, a column store built for large scans. In our measurement the stack held 2.60–2.64 GiB of memory at idle. Its Docker Compose guide recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 16 GiB RAM, with about 100 GiB of disk.

The TypeScript path is built on OpenTelemetry. You start the OTel Node SDK with LangfuseSpanProcessor, wrap the client with observeOpenAI, and wrap your own functions with observe:

This file adds 31 lines and removes 5, and installs four packages. We pinned the OTel Node SDK to 0.223.0, because @langfuse/otel 6.1.1 does not accept 0.300.0.

Langfuse successfully recreated the same trace tree, neatly tagging the spans as AGENT, GENERATION, and TOOL. It captured all the essentials: tool calls, tool definitions, and the complete message history. However, for the LLM output, it only saved the assistant's message—dropping the finish_reason, response ID, and the provider name.

We ran our deployment in Langfuse v4's events_only mode, which turns off the v1 trace endpoint. Because of this, the API didn't return a centralized trace object or root-level sums for tokens and costs, even though the UI calculated and displayed them perfectly (we didn't test other modes).

Costs showed up exactly as expected once we added a custom price entry. Since Langfuse calculates prices based on the specific usage types you define, and we only set rates for input and output, the separate reasoning tokens went unpriced. Finally, during our error test, the observe wrapper let the error bubble up to the agent, correctly flagging both the tool and the root span as an ERROR.

Phoenix self-hosts as two containers, one Python server and Postgres. In our measurement it held 0.47 GiB at idle. Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, so it is not open source. Authentication is off until you turn it on.

The TypeScript path uses Phoenix's register() helper and the OpenInference instrumentation for the OpenAI package. OpenInference is a set of OpenTelemetry attribute names for LLM spans. traceAgent and traceTool wrap the run and the tools:

This file adds 32 lines and removes 3, and installs three packages.

Phoenix rebuilt the same tree, typed as AGENT, LLM and TOOL. Each LLM span keeps the full OpenAI response object, plus the messages as flattened attributes. The root span stores no token count, but Phoenix computes a sum for the root and the trace when you read it. Cost and those sums are only in the GraphQL API and the UI, and the REST API has no per-trace endpoint.

Cost appeared after a custom price entry under Settings > Models, and Phoenix priced the reasoning tokens by falling back to the output price. In the error run, the tool span and the root were marked ERROR, and the tool span carried an exception event with the stack trace.

Opik self-hosts as eight containers, including ClickHouse, MySQL and ZooKeeper. In our measurement it held 3.69 GiB at idle, the most of the four. The self-hosted UI opened without a login, so every trace was readable from any machine that could reach the port.

The TypeScript path wraps the client with trackOpenAI and your own functions with track. By default trackOpenAI starts a new trace for every model call, so the file passes the run's span through the documented parent option:

This file adds 33 lines and removes 5. It installs opik-openai 2.2.142, and npm adds opik 1.11.14 as its peer, because opik-openai asks for opik ^1.8.61.

Opik successfully recreated the trace tree, and its trace object neatly tallies token counts across all LLM spans. In the logs, tool arguments are bundled into an array, and the LLM output only retains the assistant's message.

We did notice a quirk with the documented OpenAI wrapper (tested on the npm package opik 1.11.14): it tags model calls as general rather than llm, which incorrectly leaves the llm_span_count at zero. (We didn't test newer Opik core versions to see if this has changed). Additionally, because our synchronous tools execute in under a millisecond, they log the exact same start time as the subsequent LLM call, causing the UI to list the LLM call first out of order.

Cost tracking is entirely manual. Opik showed no costs by default, and the documentation doesn't mention a custom price table. We checked the configuration tabs on our 2.2.52 instance (Feedback definitions, AI Providers, Workspace preferences) and found no model pricing settings. To see costs, you have to manually assign a price to each individual span yourself—only the spans we hardcoded this way displayed a cost.

Finally, error reporting is highly detailed. If something fails, Opik attaches an error_info block—complete with the error type, message, and full traceback—directly to the tool span, the root span, and the overall trace.

AcruxCore self-hosts as five containers: Postgres, Redis, a Node API and worker, and nginx. In our measurement it held 0.39 GiB at idle, the least of the four. Its quickstart leaves sign-up open and ships a committed default GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which encrypts stored provider keys; replace it. We tested a local build from 2026-09-17.

The TypeScript path AcruxCore's docs put first is its gateway. The official openai client keeps working: you point its baseURL at ACRUXCORE_BASE_URL + "/gateway" and call a model registered in AcruxCore, which forwards each call to an OpenAI-compatible provider. The gateway records every model call as an llm span. The SDK's step helpers add the rest: traces.step opens the agent span, traces.wrap wraps each tool, and two headers file the gateway's spans under the agent span:

This file adds 30 lines and removes 5, and installs one package. It builds its own client, so it does not use provider.ts. The gateway refused our team API key, so the client uses a gateway virtual key created in the dashboard.

On this path every model call passes through the AcruxCore server, which none of the other four tools need. If you do not want a proxy in the request path, the SDK's register() helper sends OpenTelemetry spans from your process instead. On that path the step helpers do not join the openai package's spans, so you write the agent and tool spans by hand.

AcruxCore rebuilt the same tree, typed as agent, llm and tool, in call order. Each LLM span keeps the full response, the provider and the cached-token count, and the trace carries a token total. The LLM spans do not keep the tool definitions sent to the model, and no reasoning-token count was recorded. The trace took its name from the question, not from the agent span, and each LLM span is named by its start time.

Cost appeared on every LLM span and as a sum on the trace, from the custom price we set on the model in AcruxCore's model list. In the error run, the step helpers marked the tool span and the agent root as error with the error message, with no status code of ours. The API returned no stack trace.

All five tools accept traces over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry wire format. trace-otel.ts sends the same spans with no vendor package: the OTel Node SDK, the OTLP/HTTP protobuf exporter and the OpenInference OpenAI instrumentation. The exporter reads its endpoint and headers from environment variables:

We ran the two-tool question once per backend and changed only environment variables: the endpoint, the headers, and for Phoenix a resource attribute that sets the project name (without it, spans go to a default project). "Accepted" means the exporter reported success, which it does only for an HTTP 2xx, and we read the spans back through each API.

Opik stored the root and tool spans as general although AGENT and TOOL kinds were sent; the cause is Not tested. LangSmith mapped AGENT to its chain type. If you instrument with plain OTel and OpenInference attributes, your raw spans are not tied to one vendor, but span types, cost and trace views still differ by backend.

The first table covers setup: how much server each tool needs, how much code we changed in the agent, and how cost and the plain OTel exporter worked. Phoenix and AcruxCore had the smallest servers, and AcruxCore needed the fewest lines among the self-hosted tools. Opik was the only one without a price table.

The second table checks each trace against what LangSmith recorded for the same run, one field at a time. All five rebuilt the same tree with tokens and durations. They differ in span types, how much of the LLM output they keep, where token sums live, and how much detail they store for the failing tool.

Token totals for the two-tool question ranged from 1,910 to 2,111. Each tool traced a separate run and reasoning length varies, so these numbers do not compare the tools.

All five tools successfully traced our test agent, so the right choice really comes down to your team's specific constraints, infrastructure preferences, and how tracing fits into the rest of your MLOps tooling.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree. The real deciding factors are boilerplate code, span typing, cost tracking, and server bloat.

LangSmith remains the simplest option for LangChain users who can utilize the cloud. Otherwise, your choice depends on your priorities: Langfuse for community size, Phoenix for a lightweight Postgres footprint, Opik for strict Apache-2.0 compliance with deep error logging, or AcruxCore for combined tracing and tool governance on minimal hardware. Best of all, if you stick to standard OpenTelemetry spans, you aren't locked in—you can try them all and easily pivot later.

#10412. Is Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress standing on the ‘glass cliff’ that sets women up to fail?

Nvidia has a new interim CEO in the wake of a massive scandal. Following Jensen Huang’s highly publicized affair and subsequent resignation, the company’s longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress stepped into the role.

Kress has been at the company for 13 years after being personally recruited by Huang himself. And she’s endlessly impressive. Not only is she one of a very small number of CFO billionaires, she’s worked exceptionally closely with Huang, and made herself invaluable as a familiar face to Wall Street and is an expert at explaining the company’s plans to investors.

It goes without saying that, no matter how well equipped, the new CEO has some giant shoes to fill as Nvidia cofounder Huang’s 33-year tenure ends. However, inserting a woman into a burdensome leadership role during a time of absolute crisis isn’t exactly a new tactic. 

While women and minorities are promoted to leadership positions less often than men, there is one time when they are asked to lead more often: when massive challenges are afoot.

The Glass Cliff

The phenomenon is referred to as, not punching a hole in a glass ceiling, but rather, standing on the edge of the glass cliff. That’s because, while the promotion itself might look like a win for women in business, the precarious position the new leader steps into often sets her up for failure.

The term itself came from researchers at the University of Exeter in the UK, whose research on 100 companies found that women promoted to leadership roles during times of crisis can face intense challenges. But they often are installed so that they can act as a kind of scapegoat for the company when they fail to extinguish the wildfires, which, in this case (and often), were started by the male predecessors.

Martin Lanik, CEO of Pinsight, said, per Investopedia, that in these instances, the new woman leader can actually shield men from blame. “In times of crisis, companies don’t want to risk the loss of who they believe to be their most valuable, high-potential talent—white men. In tough times, they are more likely to sacrifice employees who they perceive as less valued and more dispensable—women and racial minorities.”

In other words, the female leader, no matter how capable, might be viewed as disposable, even as she works to manage a crisis of epic proportions.

Is a massive PR crisis what it takes for a woman to be asked to lead major tech companies?

While Kress’ glass cliff scenario is crystal clear, given the scale of the scandal, the silver lining may be that there is finally a woman at the head of a massive tech company, which are almost exclusively helmed by men like Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, Tim Cook, and Sam Altman.

Kress is anything but unqualified. But men still rule the tech world by a landslide. Therefore, the new CEO’s promotion begs the question: is this what it takes for women to be asked to lead powerful tech companies?

Christina Lindley, founder and CEO of VPRG Consulting, tells Fast Company that women deserve to lead powerful companies, but not just in order to change the narrative. “If you trust a woman to clean up a crisis, you can trust her to lead before there is one,” Lindley explains.

The founder says she wouldn’t be quick to assume that Kress is being set up to fail, given she’s so uniquely qualified for the role, but that it will be interesting to see whether “she gets the accountability without the power.” If so, Lindley says that’s not a true promotion, but “a clean up assignment.”

Lindley notes Kress’ role should come with a shot at the permanent position.

“A real leadership opportunity means she gets to shape what comes next,” the founder says.

Meanwhile, while Kress will undoubtedly have her work cut out for her, it’s hard to say whether she will be in the role for long. The company says it’s searching for a permanent CEO and will “consider internal and external candidates.”

Whether Kress becomes the permanent CEO will likely depend on how she manages the PR storm. Still, some say that companies—including the most massive tech firms—would be wise to insert more women to lead them.

Annie Scranton, founder and CEO of Pace PR, tells Fast Company, “If tech companies, and American businesses in general, want to avoid crises moving forward, they should put more women in leadership positions.”

Scranton adds, “We don’t suffer from the same lapses in judgment as men.”

Prusa has patched all the vulnerabilities discovered ahead of a coordinated news release.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Software engineer Yannick Dixken spent a week attacking his Prusa MK4S 3D printer in the name of science. At the end of the relatively short but intense period, he produced a video demonstrating the ability to Rickroll the printer via remote code execution (RCE). Dixken shared the video and findings – charting “roughly 23 individual defects” with Prusa and published his amusing but detailed Never gonna print you up! blog in coordination with the 3D printer maker. Yes, all the vulnerabilities are now patched in the Buddy firmware versions >7.0.0.

Dixken is an experienced Freelance Cloud Architect, DevOps and Platform Engineer. Security research is more of a hobby, he notes in the blog post, but it is clearly a passion strong enough to spend a whole week probing the MK4S for vulnerabilities. The result is far more than the funny old Rickroll. The week of debugging, fuzzing and reverse engineering “armed with Opus 4.8 and a fuzzer” resulted in “14 findings, roughly 23 individual defects, and a chain that ends with the printer's main controller running code I sent it over the network,” noted Dixken. “Yup, fully fledged RCE.”

The headlining RCE scored 8.1 and is officially described as High Severity. This serious bug was in the cloud (or self-hosted) management platform called Prusa Connect. You can see proof-of-concept code Rickrolling the user in Dixken’s embedded video. He sent this video to Prusa.

The methods used to uncover these vulnerabilities are outlined in the source blog, if you’d like to know more. Meanwhile, there were many other vulnerabilities uncovered and cataloged. These include a USB filename attack, heap overflows triggered by malformed encrypted print files, and network denial-of-service flaws. Many of the bugs were probably symptoms of the original developers’ use of assert statements to enforce assumptions.

Happily for Prusa 3D printer users, Dixken has responsibly disclosed this multitude of vulnerabilities. The engineer says that within 24 hours of the Rickroll video being shared on social media, the 3D printing firm’s team coordinated professionally, efficiently, and kindly. Companies don’t always react so positively to those helping them find vulnerabilities in their wares.

#10409. U.S. home sales slumped to the slowest pace in more than 16 years

Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes slumped in October to their slowest pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates climbed sharply, ratcheting up borrowing costs for aspiring homebuyers.

Existing home sales fell 5.5% last month from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday. That’s the slowest annual sales pace since August 2010, when the market was still reeling from the late-2000s U.S. housing crash.

Sales sank 8.8% compared with October last year. The latest sales tally fell short of the 3.8 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet.

“It is just a tough market for buyers and sellers,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist.

Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2 million. October is the third month in a row that the annual sales pace has remained below 4 million.

The sharp pullback in sales comes as the average rate on a 30-year mortgage climbed above 7% in September and hit its highest level in nearly three years last month.

Despite the latest pullback in sales, home prices continued to march higher nationally last month, albeit at a slower clip. The U.S. median sales price rose 0.4% in October from a year earlier to $416,700, an all-time high for the month of October based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis every month going back to July 2023.

The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Yun expects home sales this year will likely end up lower than in 2025.

This year, sales have been in a rut in large part due to rising mortgage rates, which have risen sharply in the months since the war between the U.S. and Iran started in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher.

The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage reached 7.4% early last month, its highest level in nearly three years. It briefly dipped below 6% before the war started.

While rates have eased since then, the average rate has stayed above 7% and could remain elevated. Persistently high inflation has raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September.

The central bank doesn’t set mortgage rates, but its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately influence rates on home loans.

“With sales at a 16-year low, and the Fed poised to raise rates further, housing will remain under pressure for some time,” Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets Economic Research, wrote in a note Thursday.

Many of the homes purchased last month likely went under contract in September and August, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.65% to 7.03%, according to Freddie Mac.

The sharp rise in mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, has led many would-be home shoppers to put their home shopping plans on hold.

First-time buyers accounted for just 29% of home purchases last month, down from 31% in September and 32% in October last year, NAR said. Historically, first-time buyers make up closer to 40% of home sales.

However, those who can afford to buy at current rates, or pay all cash, have a much wider selection of homes to choose from than they’ve had in years as properties sit on the market longer.

Although home inventory levels remain below historical norms, there were 1.59 million unsold homes at the end of last month — the highest level of unsold inventory on the market since November 2019, NAR said.

All told, unsold home inventory rose 1.3% last month from September and climbed 4.6% from October last year, NAR said.

October’s month-end inventory translates to a 5.1-months’ supply at the current sales pace, the largest since November 2015. Traditionally, a 4- to 6-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers.

A more balanced market gives home shoppers potentially more leverage in negotiating better terms with sellers, especially if a property has not fetched offers in weeks or months.

Last month, the national median home listing price fell 2.2% from a year earlier to $415,000 as about 20.5% of listings had their initial price lowered, according to Realtor.com.

—Alex Veiga, AP business writer

Rebooted by Hileeq has shared how others can get cheap Lenovo ThinkPads and save them from becoming e-waste by using a simple BIOS unlock hack that only requires a $10 programmer and another laptop or PC. The technique is niche, known mostly by technicians, but Hileeq is the first to give this bypass mass attention with an easy-to-follow YouTube tutorial.

Rebooted by Hileeq's channel, dedicated to fixing cheap eBay finds, documents the process and what he learned while fixing the laptops. Three weeks ago, he posted a video explaining how to bypass locked Lenovo ThinkPads with Intel 4th- to 8th-generation CPUs using a cheap CH431A programmer to read, write, erase, and save EEPROM and SPI flash memory.

Companies often add supervisor passwords to the fleet of ThinkPads they hand out to their employees as an IT security measure. When these ThinkPads are disposed of, often with the storage removed and destroyed, it’s rare that the supervisor passwords are included and documented. These locked ThinkPads are then incredibly cheap because of the lack of access, ending up as e-waste most of the time. However, Victor Voinea shared a post in a Romanian forum containing his ThinkPad supervisor removal exploits.

Unfortunately, Voinea’s method generated a random password every time the exploit was run, requiring users to contact Voinea for the key specific to the generated hardware ID — and getting the password wasn’t free. However, in 2020, Knucklegrumble posted a free way to bypass the password in the Badcaps electronics repair forum. Mark Juvan, an Ethical Hacker, reverse-engineered Knucklegrumble’s exploit as his cybersecurity master’s thesis at Radboud University Nijmegen, Netherlands, which goes into deeper detail.

The exploit begins by extracting the BIOS from the EEPROM chip on the motherboard using the CH341A programmer and plugging it into a USB port of another PC or laptop. Hileeq then uses NeoProgrammer, a utility for CH341A programmers, and dumps the BIOS, saving a copy of it on the other laptop. NeoProgrammer then applies the same auto-patching workflow Knucklegrumble created.

When the patched BIOS is flashed onto the EEPROM, the laptop can then be turned on, and Hileeq goes through some steps requiring a few keystrokes which remove the password saved in the Embedded Controller (EC), a separate IC that stores security data, among other system tasks. The original BIOS can then be flashed back into the EEPROM, and with the supervisor password removed, the laptop is now usable.

Juvan states in his paper that the exploit takes advantage of a weakness in Lenovo’s firmware verification and driver architecture. Lenovo actually provides the EmulatedEepromDxe driver needed by the exploit, and the driver allows the EEPROM to be read and written to — and the EC’s supervisor password happens to be stored where it’s treated as EEPROM memory, allowing the supervisor password to be overwritten or removed.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The hard, complicated work has already been done by the electronics repair community, and now the process to bypass the supervisor password requires just a few steps and an inexpensive programmer tool. While the method may only be for ThinkPads with Intel 4th- to 8th-generation CPUs, this will still save plenty of usable ThinkPads from going to waste, as Hileeq’s popular post potentially encourages more people to attempt this themselves — who knows, this might cause a domino effect to unlock newer generations of ThinkPads.

#10405. Jensen Huang has argued execs need less supervision. Then a scandal made him step down as Nvidia CEO

The spectacular downfall of superstar Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who resigned this morning after admitting to an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy and amid reports of another affair with one of his executives—casts a harsh light on a key tenet of Huang’s own management philosophy: that senior executives need little supervision.

Huang often used this belief to justify Nvidia’s unique management structure, in which 50 to 60 senior executives reported directly to him, arguing that senior leaders have a proven ability to make decisions, manage people, and solve problems on their own.

“CEOs should have the most reports by definition, because the people that report to the CEO require the least amount of management,” he said during an appearance at Stanford Graduate School of Business in 2024. “It makes no sense to me that CEOs have so few people reporting to them.”

The approach, which Huang often reiterated in public appearances, reflects a broader Silicon Valley ideal: hire extraordinary people and give them free rein to do their best work. A classic example is Google’s 20%-time policy, which allowed employees to spend a portion of their time exploring their own ideas and innovations.  

Huang’s abrupt exit shows the drawbacks of this philosophy—at least when it comes to the behavior of top executives. While experienced leaders may not require micromanagement, allowing them to operate with very little oversight exposes organizations to major risks.

As Huang’s actions have illustrated, even the most capable executives can show extremely poor personal judgment. This may be especially true in corporate cultures like Nvidia’s, where the line between the personal and the professional is often blurred. 

Over the years, reports have described Nvidia as an intensely personal workplace in which Huang regularly interrogated junior employees about their work, sent emails late into the night, and exerted enormous influence over the company’s culture.

Senior leaders also have fewer people who are willing to rein in their behavior—something that was clearly the case at Nvidia. Last spring, proxy advisory firm Institutional Shareholder Services assigned its riskiest rating to Nvidia’s board structure. According to The Wall Street Journal, ISS cited the board’s multiple long-tenured directors, its lack of a chairman, the absence of a mechanism to refresh the board, and other factors.

Finally, the consequences of misconduct increase with seniority. In Huang’s case, the fallout could extend even beyond Nvidia, which manufactures chips crucial to the AI boom and has been central to American leadership in the area.

Management theorists have long struggled to balance meaningful oversight with executives’ autonomy, and some have concluded that no one-size-fits-all approach ensures proper board oversight. Boards must tailor oversight to individual CEOs and circumstances rather than mechanically applying standardized rules.

In Nvidia’s case, at least, the board failed to properly assess the risks of Huang’s personal behavior or plan adequately for succession. And the lesson for others is clear: while senior executives don’t need micromanagement, they still need someone to answer to.

#10404. Everything you wanted to know about Nvidia but were too afraid to ask

If you’re not in the tech world, you might only have been vaguely aware of Nvidia—and CEO Jensen Huang’s leather jackets—until he admitted to having an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. On November 12, a day after revelations of a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive, Huang resigned. Here’s why the company’s future could affect the entire AI industry.

What Nvidia does

Nvidia is at the center of the AI boom, as the world’s largest supplier of chips used in AI data centers. By some estimates, the company controls 80% of the market. As of November 3, it was the most valuable company in the world, with a market cap of around $5 trillion. By the morning of November 12, as Nvidia’s stock continued to plummet, that figure dropped to $4 trillion. (Huang’s own net worth had fallen $7.4 billion by that point.)

Huang and cofounders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem launched the company in 1993. They started making graphics processing units, better known as GPUs, for video games. In 2006, they rolled out a platform that enabled other uses for GPUs. In 2012, researchers used the company’s chips to train AlexNet, a breakthrough AI program that taught computers how to recognize images. By the time that ChatGPT launched, Nvidia’s tech was fundamental to AI development.

A large data center might have tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs that run calculations to train AI models and generate responses when you type a question into ChatGPT or Claude. Training a new AI model could sometimes involve as many as 100,000 GPUs running at the same time for months. After the model is trained, the GPUs are used for “inference,” or applying the trained model to, say, rewrite your email or draw a cartoon of your cat. Inference also requires huge numbers of GPUs given that millions of people use AI at the same time. (In the U.S., around 60 million people use AI chatbots every day, according to a Pew survey this summer.)

Nvidia systems also include CPUs (central processing units) that coordinate tasks and run operating systems in data centers, along with networking equipment that lets GPUs communicate. Its software coordinates the GPUs.

Huang’s downfall

It’s not clear when Jensen Huang started his affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a woman who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of being a Chinese spy. The Chinese government has denied that she is a spy.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became an Nvidia customer. Megaspeed reportedly smuggled Nvidia’s chips into China, bypassing U.S. sanctions. The U.S. first restricted the export of Nvidia’s chips to China in 2022, citing the risk that China could use them for military development and to compete in AI. Alice Huang reportedly helped move $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China.

The New York Times first reported on the relationship and the spy allegations on October 29, and Jensen Huang initially said that it was an ordinary business relationship, not an affair. On November 6, the Financial Times reported that it was a romantic relationship. Two days later, Jensen Huang sent an email to Nvidia employees admitting that it had been an affair.

On November 11, reports emerged that Huang also had an affair with one of his employees at Nvidia, reportedly Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. On November 12, as pressure mounted from Nvidia’s board, Huang announced his resignation.

Why Jensen Huang can’t easily be replaced

It’s not simple for someone else to step into Huang’s shoes. He was directly involved in decisions that most executives would delegate, from managing in detail how Nvidia’s products were built to how salespeople talked to customers. A typical CEO might have five or 10 direct reports; Huang had as many as 60 direct reports. He reportedly sent hundreds of emails a day.

He had an unusual level of control—and no plan in place for succession. After Huang resigned, Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement. It’s not clear what will happen next. But it’s possible that the company’s strategic decisions about products, manufacturing, and customers could slow down. Huang oversaw how Nvidia’s full system was integrated, not just its GPUs. The next leader may not have the same vision for the product. Relationships with customers might deteriorate. There might be internal struggles for control.

A circular business model—and potential fallout for AI companies

Nvidia sells its technology to companies like Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI. (OpenAI and others also use it indirectly by leasing space in third-party data centers.) But Nvidia is also investing heavily in the artificial intelligence ecosystem. It committed $30 billion to OpenAI’s financing round and guaranteed up to $105 billion for an Ohio data center that would serve OpenAI. It sells GPUs to AI infrastructure company CoreWeave, but has also invested in the company, including a $2 billion investment in January. Nvidia also agreed to purchase up to $6.3 billion of CoreWeave’s unused computing capacity over the next several years and has struck similar deals to buy cloud computing services from its customers. Meanwhile, it has partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, and other asset managers to mobilize financing for AI infrastructure.

Anthropic, which has plans to file for its IPO next week, is also tightly entangled with Nvidia. Nvidia committed to invest up to $10 billion in the company in 2025; Anthropic committed to use up to 1 gigawatt of Nvidia computing capacity. Nvidia was reportedly considering billions of dollars in credit guarantees for a new data center for Anthropic. It also had reported plans to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic’s IPO.

All of this meant Nvidia was helping prop up demand for its own technology, making it harder to gauge how quickly AI would have grown on the strength of the underlying economics alone. Huang personally spearheaded these investments and partnerships, and it’s unclear whether his successor will be as willing to finance Nvidia’s customers. That uncertainty could slow some of the AI industry’s planned expansion.
